why: A prospect on a six-year-old domain follows up a booking made through her public intro page and shares reports on his own domain, with nothing asked of her beyond the call.
A 16-day-old domain uses her sailing interest and the quay to harvest her weight, home postcode and phone number under a crew-matching pretext.
A young startup founder whose domain age fits his story asks only for feedback on his talk-inspired idea, with no link beyond his homepage and no request for data or money.
An SMS impersonating her association pushes an urgent proxy-vote link on a 6-day-old domain.
An unexpected overdue-invoice chase from a printer whose domain is five weeks old, sending her to a pay link.
An AGM proxy form hosted on a 24-day-old lookalike association domain rather than the association's own.
A 4-week-old domain stitches together her podcast, notes page and sailing to pull her off her booking page onto a private phone line and a confidential document drop.
A routine, unchanged £60 subscription notice from the association's 16-year-old domain, with standing bank details and no link or urgency.
A 6-day-old domain baits her with a board role built from her role and tenure, then asks her to send back an SMS code sent to her phone, which is an account-takeover move.
A standard new-device sign-in notice from a ten-year-old service domain, with no link and nothing to do unless the sign-in was not hers.
A listener writing from an old webmail provider asks for paid advice about a family trust, with no link, attachment or request for data.
The sender uses the School's real domain, but the message asks for her existing alumni login on a 6-week-old outside domain, so she should confirm with the alumni office before signing in.
A WhatsApp message claiming to be Harborlight liaison pushes an urgent slide upload to a one-week-old lookalike domain instead of the forum's own.
An FYI-only note from the podcast's own seven-year-old domain about a sponsor read, asking for nothing.
A 3-week-old regatta domain thanks her for interest she may never have shown and sends her to an entry link, so she should check it with the club first.
An SMS claiming to be her charter body threatens suspension unless she replies with a verification code, which is a classic code-theft takeover.
A 4-day-old lookalike association domain asks her to email back a one-time code sent to her mobile, under a Friday deadline.
A follow-up to a meeting she can confirm, booked through her own page, from a domain whose age matches the stated recent incorporation, with nothing asked of her.
A 4-day-old lookalike of her firm's domain impersonates a colleague on her personal email to set up an off-record favour, which is the opening of a CEO-fraud play.
A plain club ask to cover race-officer duty, with no link, payment or data request.
The podcast host, writing from the show's established domain, invites an optional follow-up answer, with no link or request for data.
A designer's invoice for work she can confirm, payable to the same bank details as the existing quote, with no change of details and no urgency.
The forum's 14-year-old domain asks permission before sharing only her already-public contact page or booking link.
A routine speaker-release request from the forum's own long-standing domain, with the option to keep the recording unlisted.
A photo-tag notice from a sailing club domain nearly three years old, linking only to its own site and asking for nothing.
A personal status update with no link or request, so there is nothing to act on beyond the information.
A 15-day-old lookalike of the podcast's domain lures her to a transcript-review link that does not sit on thornbeckhour.com.
A charter-renewal invoice from an 8-day-old payments lookalike domain, with a pay link and bank details.
